title: Forecasting root-zone soil moisture with low-cost capacitive sensors for smallholder irrigation scheduling

headings.text: Forecasting root-zone soil moisture with low-cost capacitive sensors for smallholder irrigation scheduling

key_sentences: Smallholder farmers rarely have access to the soil moisture information that irrigation scheduling requires.
A simple water-balance model driven by these readings forecast the next irrigation date within one day in 83% of cases.
This practice wastes water when the soil is still wet and stresses the crop when hot weather dries the soil faster than expected.
The trials took place in two irrigation schemes on sandy loam and clay loam soils.
Two sensors were buried in each plot, at depths of 15 cm and 35 cm.
It adds rainfall and irrigation, subtracts crop evapotranspiration, and resets the stored water to the sensor value each morning.
Errors were larger on the clay loam, where shrinkage cracks occasionally separated the sensor from the soil.
Forecasts were least reliable after heavy rain, when drainage below the root zone was overestimated.
The water savings did not reduce yields, which suggests that calendar irrigation applied more water than the crops could use.
Combined with a transparent water-balance model, they gave forecasts that farmers understood and trusted.
